sex_rules.male: men only, on every case the sources show
sex_rules.female: women only, on every case the sources show

bases.attested_in_the_layer: a business record in this project names a hand of this kind
bases.directory_1839: Fergus's 1839 directory, read by T-1346, counts the trade
bases.period_convention: the project holds no figure; the row is reconstructed from the practice of the trade and names its analogue

vocabularies.age_bands_are_this_model_s_own: These say what age a kind of hand was. The residents layer's age bands say how a card's age was EVIDENCED. They are different questions and this file does not mix them.

clerks_per_commerce_principal.what_it_is: clerks per PERSON in a commerce trade, not per establishment — the directory counts people and prints no houses. It is the WIDE reading, and it divides by tavern and livery keepers who kept no counting house; the like-for-like ratio below is the one the reconciliation uses, and this one stands beside it so that the narrowing is visible.
clerks_per_commerce_principal.date_caution: 1839 IS FOUR YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, and this volume is Fergus's 1876 completion of a list that, in the compiler's own words, "was never written". Every share below is the shape of a LATER town recalled later still. It is a prior for a draw and it is not a count of 1835, nor evidence about any person in it.

clerks_per_clerk_employing_principal.what_it_is: the same 152 clerks over only those 1839 trades that this model's class table sends to an establishment with a clerk in it. A trade the 1839 list counts and this town holds no record of — the banker, the ship chandler — falls out of the denominator with the taverns, and that is a NARROWING: it raises the ratio and so flatters the model. It is used because it is the only comparison in matching units, and the wide reading above is printed so the reader can take the other view.

the_directory_did_not_canvass_service.finding: 50 keepers of taverns, boarding houses and refectories stand in the 1839 list against 2 bar-keepers, 5 domestics and 1 laundress. No hostler, cook or chambermaid is printed at all. That is a list of householders, so it is a FLOOR for service labour and never a count — which is why every service row in this model is `period_convention`.

staff_roles.note: A sale is cried by the auctioneer and booked by somebody. 9 auctioneers in 1839.
A porter on sale days. Analogue: the stores above.
11 bakers in 1839. A bakehouse is worked at night and the hand sleeps there.
A boy on the delivery basket. Analogue: the bakehouse above.
A book store is a store. `either`: the trade is one of the few a town of this date let a woman keep counter in, and the directory refuses neither.
3 brewers in 1839 for 2 breweries in the 1835 census — the principals only; the mash was worked by hands the list booked as labourers.
16 butchers in 1839 against the one shop and the market here.
13 druggists in 1839 and the commerce clerk share over them. The druggist's clerk is often reading medicine, which is why he boards in the house.

The counting-house clerk is the one role the directory counts in bulk — 152 of them, the largest single trade in the 1839 list after the carpenters — and the printed forms name their houses outright ('clerk stiles burton'). A young man boarding with his employer or over the store is the ordinary arrangement; half is this model's reading of 'often', and it is a reading.
A porter to shift goods, at the larger houses only. Analogue: the 1839 list's seven porters, counted under labourer, against 151 commerce principals.
The forwarding house is the heaviest clerical trade on the river: 15 forwarding and commission principals in 1839 and the bookkeepers counted with the clerks.

Warehousemen: the 1839 list prints the term only twice, which is the floor and not the count — a warehouse on the South Water landings was worked by hands the directory booked as labourers, of whom it counts 73.
41 teamsters and 30 draymen in 1839, against a river trade this one grew out of.
12 founders in 1839. A furnace is the largest hand-count of any shop in town.
A grocery is a smaller counting house than a dry-goods store and the low end is the keeper alone. Same clerk calibration, one step down.
A hand for barrels and the drayage. Analogue: as above.
Counted with the commerce clerks; the trade is a store whatever it sells.
A stove dealer who fits and repairs keeps a tinner. Analogue: the town's own tin and copper manufactories, which the census counts separately.
25 land agents in 1839; the office is the principal and his papers, and a clerk only at the busiest.
The student-at-law, who read in an office rather than at a school. Analogue: the 1839 list's 11 students against 45 attorneys, a quarter of them.

classes.reads_as: a saddler's and harness maker's shop

staff_roles.note: 6 harness makers in 1839 against 3 shops here.
Analogue: the journeyman row above.
Hostlers. `hostler` is outside the vocabulary; see `vocabulary_gaps`. Analogue: the 11 livery stable keepers of 1839, against whom the list prints no hostler.
The stable boy. Analogue: as above.
A yard is piled and loaded by hand. Analogue: the forwarding houses above, whose warehouse labour this model prices the same way.
6 sawyers and 7 millers in 1839; a steam saw-mill is a gang and not a man.
The needle trades ran on assistants and the 1835 notices advertise for them. Analogue: the 1839 list's six milliners and its tailoresses, and the 1840 column that has no row for them at all.
A girl bound to the needle, living in. Analogue: as above.
14 painters in 1839; the trade works in pairs.
Analogue: the journeyman row above.
A physician's student, on the same footing as the law student. Analogue: as above.
An assistant in the office. Analogue: the two postmasters of 1839.

Journeymen at case and press. The 1839 list counts 15 printers — compositors, pressmen and job printers — against 2 editors, and the two offices of the 1835 census are the establishments those hands worked in four years earlier.

The apprentice, who lives in. Analogue: the journeyman row above; the project holds no roll of the Democrat's or the American's hands — see docs/RESEARCH/chicago_democrat_office.md, which reads the imprint and no roll.
An assistant, at the larger schools only; the town's schools of 1835 are one room and one teacher. Analogue: the 1839 list's 13 schoolteachers.
27 shoemakers in 1839 against 8 shops here.
Analogue: the journeyman row above.

classes.reads_as: a jeweller's, hatter's or confectioner's shop

staff_roles.note: A jeweller's, hatter's or confectioner's is a one-hand shop at this date. Analogue: the 1839 list's 7 watchmakers and 5 hatters, none with a counted hand.
The striker, who swings while the smith holds. Analogue: the 1839 list's 48 smiths in a town that had 5 shops in 1835.
A bound boy. Analogue: as above.
8 soap and candle makers in 1839 across a handful of works.
Chainmen, hired by the survey and not by the year. Analogue: the 13 surveyors of 1839, against whom the list prints no chainman.
42 tailors in 1839 against 7 tailoring houses here.
The tailoress, who sewed what the cutter cut. Analogue: the 1839 list's printed 'cloak maker and tailoress', counted under tailor, and the millinery rows above.
Analogue: the journeyman row above.

The bar-keeper. `bar_keeper` is NOT in the residents occupation vocabulary and is carried here under the nearest term it does hold; see `vocabulary_gaps`. Analogue: the 1839 list's two bar-keepers against 50 keepers of houses — a floor, and the clearest evidence in this file that the directory did not canvass service.
The hostler, who is a house's stable. `hostler` is outside the vocabulary. Analogue: the livery stables below, and the 1839 list's silence.
The cook. A house that feeds travellers cooks every day of the week. Analogue: the 1839 list's five domestics against a town of 4,000 — a floor, not a count.
Chambermaids, by the number of beds. Analogue: the lodging model's per-place capacities, which this row does not itself read.
The boy — boots, errands, the yard. Analogue: as above.
8 tinsmiths in 1839; the census counts 2 manufactories in 1835.
Analogue: the journeyman row above.

the_shop_household_rule.rule: `lives_on_premises` is the share of holders of a role who slept in the proprietor's house or over the shop, and `household_relationship` is the term their card carries in that household. A clerk at 0.5 means half the clerks of that class are household members of their employer and half keep their own lodging or board elsewhere.
the_shop_household_rule.not_a_seating: A share is not a bed. The lodging model (T-1370) owns capacity and T-1371 owns who sleeps where; this rule only says which staff are candidates for the employer's household.

dry_run.not_a_roster: Counts of ROLES over establishments. No person is named, drawn or written; T-1189 does that and this is the quota it does it to.

on_the_wide_ratio_instead.note: The wide ratio divides the same clerks by tavern, livery and boarding-house keepers as well, and on it the model looks over-clerked. Printed rather than buried: it is the reading a sceptic would take.

against_the_clerk_calibration.if_it_disagrees: The per-house rules are period convention and the ratio is a 1839 measurement of a bigger town. A disagreement is STATED here and neither side is moved to close it; T-1189 spends against the rules and reports the residual.

against_the_town_model_employment.method: The 1840 schedule returns 18% of persons in its seven industry columns, 0.902 per household. Applied to this model's July population range. The 1840 columns count persons in families and not occupations of named men, so this is a size and not a roster.
against_the_town_model_employment.what_it_does_not_mean: The town model's employed persons counts EVERY working person — the labourers of the harbour works, the garrison, the farmers outside the limits, the domestic service the 1840 columns have no row for. The businesses of this layer are a PART of that figure, so falling below the low end is expected and falling above it is a refusal.

open_questions.question: Is the 1839 clerk ratio a prior for 1835 at all?
open_questions.why_it_matters: It is the only staffing figure the project holds, and 1839 is a town with a bank, a canal and four more years of growth. The model uses it to CHECK its rules and not to set them, which is the most weight it will bear.

open_questions.question: What does the town do about the service labour no source counts?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The 1840 industry columns have no row for domestic service and the 1839 directory prints five domestics. The town model already says its trade split understates household labour by an amount it cannot bound; this model reconstructs that labour for businesses and cannot bound it either.

open_questions.question: The records the layer gives no trade to.
open_questions.why_it_matters: 9 of the 179 houses standing at the scene date carry no `occupation`, so they are staffed by nobody here. T-1182's audit is what fixes that, and until it runs this model understates the town.
